\paragraph{Why quality estimators fail as selectors.}
The correlation-selection gap (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) reflects a fundamental information asymmetry.
Quality estimation ranks \textit{instances} by expected output quality, which consistency signals accomplish by measuring output distribution entropy: high inter-sample agreement indicates a peaked distribution and correlates with high F1.
Sample selection ranks \textit{candidates within a single instance}, requiring per-sample quality information that instance-level aggregation discards.
Our data quantify this directly.
On SciERC NER, the random baseline (0.580) falls only 2.9~pp below greedy (0.609), confirming that per-instance sample variance is small relative to between-instance difficulty variance; yet the oracle gap of 16.0~pp shows that better candidates exist---they differ by subtle extraction choices invisible to consistency signals.
The best quality estimator, Voting ($\rho{=}0.502$), selects to only 0.596---\textit{below} greedy---because its instance-level score cannot rank near-identical candidates.
On RE, where compound entity-then-relation decisions create more divergent outputs (oracle gap: 18.7~pp), the only per-sample signal---log-probability---achieves +2.3~pp over greedy while all instance-level signals fail.
The $\rho$--AUROC dissociation on CoNLL illuminates the same asymmetry from a metric perspective: logprob achieves the highest AUROC (0.761) yet the lowest $\rho$ (0.307), providing coarse binary separation (high AUROC) without fine-grained ranking (low $\rho$).
Both metrics measure between-instance discrimination at different granularity; neither captures within-instance variation, explaining why even high AUROC does not translate to selection ability.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.055$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ logprob $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while logprob does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.
